paragraph: To Surpanakha who was mortified Khara said, "Your humiliation makes me furious. Man and a mere mortal, Rama is no power to contend with. He shall perish this instant. Be assured that Rama and his brother will soon reach the land of Yama and you will drink their warm blood as I strike them down." Surpanakha forgetting her anger was pleased with her brother. Khara instructed Dooshana, the commander of his army to gather fourteen thousand warriors. They were to be the most fierce and ruthless who would revel in cruelty, exult in slaying and indulge in the carnage of war. These dark savage hordes were to torture, torment and tear at their enemy. "This army will be led by me, ready my chariot", said Khara. With a deafening roar, as weapons clanged, wheels rolled and hooves pounded, the army set forth. A chariot as lofty as mount Meru, with wheels of gold studded with gems carried Khara. He led the fourteen thousand men of war to kill Rama, the incarnation of Visnu. Impatient to confront his enemy he urged his charioteer to drive faster.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Surpanakha recounts her disfigurement to Khara, who, enraged by her humiliation, vows immediate revenge against Rama and Lakshmana. Khara, confident in his power and dismissive of Rama's strength, commands his army commander Dooshana to assemble a formidable force of fourteen thousand ruthless Rakshasas. Khara then personally leads this massive army in his grand chariot to confront and destroy Rama.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage illustrates the dangerous escalation of conflict driven by unchecked ego, pride, and the thirst for vengeance. Khara's overconfidence and underestimation of Rama's divine power (ironically referring to him as 'no power to contend with' while he is an incarnation of Vishnu) set the stage for a tragic downfall. The assembly of a vast, cruel army highlights the destructive nature of adharma when it mobilizes for war. Surpanakha's momentary satisfaction at the promise of revenge, forgetting her anger, shows the manipulative power of such promises.
Outcome/Resolution: Fueled by Khara's outrage and Surpanakha's desire for revenge, a massive army of fourteen thousand fierce Rakshasas, led by Khara himself, is mobilized to attack Rama and Lakshmana. They set out with great force and aggression, determined to destroy the two princes, unaware of Rama's divine nature and strength.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Krodha (Rage - Khara's primary emotion driving his actions)
Ahankara (Ego/Pride - Khara's inflated sense of power and dismissiveness of Rama)
Pratishodh (Vengeance - The underlying motivation for both Surpanakha and Khara)
Moha (Delusion/Ignorance - Khara's inability to recognize Rama's divine nature and underestimate his power)
Rakshasa Dharma/Adharma (The inherent unrighteousness and cruelty of the Rakshasa way of life, contrasted with Vishnu's incarnation purpose)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Spiritually, this passage signifies the mobilization of overwhelming Adharma (unrighteousness) against divine Dharma. Khara, driven by intense Krodha (rage) and a massive Ahankara (ego), is deluded by Moha (ignorance) into underestimating Rama, who is the incarnation of Vishnu. The assembly of fourteen thousand cruel Rakshasas, who revel in carnage, represents the peak of demonic power arrayed against righteousness. This seemingly powerful display of force is ultimately a spiritual confrontation, where ignorance and unrighteousness are poised to clash with the supreme divine power, foreshadowing the inevitable defeat of the forces of darkness.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, this scene highlights the destructive nature of unchecked anger management and inflated ego. Khara's response to Surpanakha's humiliation is a prime example of impulsive, rage-fueled decision-making, where rational assessment is overridden by a desire for immediate vengeance. His dismissive attitude towards Rama reveals a deep-seated ego and overconfidence, a common psychological pitfall leading to misjudgment. Surpanakha's temporary relief and pleasure, 'forgetting her anger,' underscore how the promise of revenge can psychologically satisfy and momentarily regulate extreme negative emotions, however fleetingly. The readiness to deploy such a vast and cruel army also reflects a collective psychological pathology of aggression and disregard for life within the Rakshasa community.
